      How it works in 3 steps

      1Select a map

      Select a satellite map from the catalog, or upload an image of your own.

      2Press Play

      The page scans the map from left to right and translates its colors into music.

        How Colors Become Music

        The page reads the map in 240 steps from left to right. At each step it samples six horizontal bands, from north to south.
        In the mapIn the soundWhat you hear
        Hue (the color itself)PitchBlue: low notes. Green and yellow: middle notes. Red: high notes. Each note is snapped to the chord or scale of the music style, so the result stays harmonious.
        Brightness (light or dark)VolumeBright colors are loud; dark colors are very quiet.
        Saturation (vivid or grayish)TimbreVivid colors yield a bright, rich timbre; muted, grayish colors yield a rounder, mellower one.
        Gray or blackSilenceLand and empty space are silent.
        The whole mapTempo, density, key and instrumentsThe overall hue, brightness, color variety, contrast and coverage of the map set the tempo, the density of the music, its pitch center, the order of the chords and the lead instrument. A calm, uniform map yields a sparse, ambient texture; a varied, high-contrast map yields a busy, energetic one.
        PositionTime and stereoLeft to right is time. The notes of each column are spread across the stereo field.

        Map Guide

        NASA satellites and computer models monitor the oceans and the atmosphere every day. Each map below displays one of these measurements and is paired with its own music style. Sound makes it possible to perceive patterns without relying on color vision.

        Guide to the maps in the catalog: what each shows, how to read its colors and its music style
        MapWhat it showsHow to read itMusic style
        Ocean currentsThe direction and speed of ocean currents.Blue and green indicate slower water; orange and red indicate faster water.Classical. The tempo increases with current speed (56 to 156 BPM).
        Sea surface temperatureThe temperature of the ocean’s surface layer.Red marks warm water near the equator; blue marks cold water near the poles. Land is black and silent.Jazz.
        Sea surface temperature anomalyHow much warmer or colder the sea surface is than normal.Dark red is much warmer than usual; blue is colder than usual. A warm band across the tropical Pacific is characteristic of El Niño conditions.Indie.
        Air temperatureNear-surface air temperature.Dark red is hottest; yellow and blue are cooler; white and purple are coldest, near Antarctica.Hip hop.
        Wind and stormsWind strength, from calm air to strong winds, including large storm systems over the Southern Ocean.Dark blue is calm; light blue, yellow and red indicate stronger winds.Heavy metal.
        Rain and cloudsThe distribution of clouds and rainfall.White is cloud. Green, blue and purple are rain; the most intense colors mark the heaviest rainfall.Rock and roll.
        HumidityThe amount of water vapor in the air.Dark blue is very humid air, mostly in the tropics; tan and brown are dry air, as over deserts and polar regions.Blues.
        Dust and aerosolsFine particles suspended in the air, such as dust, smoke and pollution.Dark orange indicates higher particle concentrations; pale yellow indicates cleaner air.Arabic music.
        Ozone (purple scale)The amount of ozone in the air. Confirm the exact variable against the NASA caption.Darker purple indicates a higher amount; gray indicates a low amount.Pop.
        Nitrogen (green scale)The amount of nitrogen in the air. Confirm the exact variable against the NASA caption.Darker green indicates a higher amount; black or white areas have little or no data.Electronic.

        Why turn data into sound?

        This approach is called sonification. Listening to a map supports people with low vision or blindness, helps children learn through music, and allows everyone to notice changes that are hard to see in an image. It also makes data more memorable in environmental awareness campaigns.

        Learn: from color to note

        Every color combines three properties, and each one shapes a different aspect of the sound. Touch, slide and listen.

        Hue = Pitch

        Blue produces low, deep notes; red produces high, bright ones.

        Brightness = Volume

        Dark colors are quiet; bright colors are loud.

        Saturation = Timbre

        Grayish colors sound soft and round; vivid colors sound rich and buzzy.

        The color keyboard

        Tap a key to hear it, played with the saturation and brightness you set below.

        Listen and guess

        A mystery note will play. Tap the color key you think produced it.

        Music styles: what each kind of data sounds like

        Each map has its own music style. The page synthesizes all of this music live, without recordings. Press “Hear it” for a short sample.

        Questions and answers

        How do I use Sealing Sounds?
        1. Select a map from the catalog, or add your own image.
        2. Press Play, or press Space. The map plays from left to right.
        3. Click or tap the map to hear a single location.
        4. Use “Describe this map” to hear a spoken description.
        Where do the maps come from?

        They come from NASA’s Earth Information Center, which documents how our planet is changing across nine themes: sea level, air quality, biodiversity, wildfires, greenhouse gases, energy, natural disasters, water resources and agriculture. This project focuses on the ocean and the atmosphere above it.

        What is the DJ mix?

        When it is on, the music changes style every eight bars, with a rising sweep and a drum roll before each transition, as in a DJ set. The notes still derive from the colors of your map.

        Glossary
        • Pitch: how high or low a note is.
        • Tempo or BPM: the speed of the music, in beats per minute.
        • Timbre: the character of a sound, such as soft or bright.
        • Pentatonic scale: a five-note scale whose notes sound consonant together (used by the color keyboard).
        • Sonification: turning data into sound.
        Who is it for?

        Blind and low-vision listeners, primary-school classes, music-therapy settings and environmental awareness campaigns.

        Can I use my own maps?

        Yes. Add any image in the “Add your own map” box. Maps with a clear color scale work best. Black and gray areas are silent.

        Does it work with a screen reader?

        Yes. Controls have descriptive labels, status messages are announced automatically, and the main actions have keyboard shortcuts.

        Shortcuts

        • Space play or pause
        • ← and → move 5 percent back or forward
        • Home start over
        • D describe the map
        • L listen to the current section

        Accessibility

        Use the toolbar at the top of every screen to adapt the page. Each option is described below.

        • Screen reader: every control has a label, and status messages are announced as they change.
        • Keyboard: every function can be operated without a mouse, and keyboard focus is always clearly visible.
        • Spoken descriptions: use “Describe this map”, or enable narration during playback. You can choose the narrator’s voice and speed.
        • Vision: larger text, a high-contrast mode and an enlarged map with zoom.
        • Sensory comfort: calm mode removes animations; soft sound lowers the volume and removes sudden accents.
        • Reading: an easy-read font with wider spacing.
        • Your own maps: you can add a description to every map you upload.
        • Orientation: a mini player stays in view as you scroll, a button returns you to the top, and the page asks for confirmation before you leave while a map is playing or if you have added your own maps.

        Declaration

        Our project and its purpose

        An interactive platform that turns geographic data into music, offering an alternative way to perceive information. Inspired by the cognitive benefits of music therapy, the tool fosters engaging learning for children, offers an accessible experience for people with low vision, and strengthens environmental awareness campaigns through the emotional impact of sound.

        Our commitment to accessibility

        Sealing Sounds is designed primarily for people with low vision or blindness and for neurodivergent users. It can be used with a screen reader, a keyboard, a touch screen or a mouse. The tools and features that put this commitment into practice are listed under Accessibility.
